title: 7 Dogs Review: Saudi Arabia's $40 Million Action Spectacle Brings Salman Khan and Sanjay Dutt Into a Globe-Trotting Thriller
excerpt: The Saudi-backed action film features a sprawling international cast including Monica Bellucci and Giancarlo Esposito, but critics say spectacle wins over story.
body:
• 7 Dogs is a $40 million Saudi-backed action thriller directed by Adil El Arbi and Bilall Fallah (Bad Boys: Ride or Die), filmed almost entirely at Al-Hisn Big Time Studios in Riyadh.
  • Salman Khan and Sanjay Dutt appear in extended cameos during a Mumbai-set chapter, while the international cast includes Monica Bellucci, Giancarlo Esposito and Martin Lawrence.
  • Critics have praised the ambitious scale and inventive camerawork but faulted the thin screenplay, underdeveloped characters, and an over-reliance on spectacle over storytelling.
  • The film is playing in India in Hindi and English, with early reviews calling it more impressive than memorable — an action spectacle that delivers thrills but lacks emotional weight.

A Saudi Showcase With Global Ambitions

Saudi Arabia's most expensive film production to date has arrived in Indian cinemas, carrying a $40 million budget, a globe-trotting plot and a cast list that reads like a who's-who of international action cinema. 7 Dogs, directed by Bad Boys duo Adil El Arbi and Bilall Fallah, brings together Egyptian superstars Ahmed Ezz and Karim Abdel Aziz alongside Monica Bellucci, Giancarlo Esposito, Martin Lawrence, Salman Khan and Sanjay Dutt.

https://x.com/bollywoodcrazis/status/2091128399419076804

The film follows Interpol agent Khalid (Ezz) who teams up with a captured kingpin Ghali (Abdel Aziz) to infiltrate a transnational crime syndicate known as the 7 Dogs. The syndicate's members are spread across Shanghai, Mumbai, Las Vegas, Riyadh and elsewhere — each chapter introducing a new location, a new villain and a new style of action set-piece.

Shot almost entirely at the expansive Al-Hisn Big Time Studios in Riyadh, the production doubles the Saudi studio for locations as diverse as Interpol headquarters, Shanghai night markets and Mumbai streets. The story was written by Turki Al-Sheikh, chairman of Saudi Arabia's General Entertainment Authority.

The Bollywood Chapter

For Indian audiences, the Mumbai segment is the obvious draw. Khan plays Jauhar, a local fixer and informant who roasts kebabs in a pinstripe suit. Dutt appears as Ranjit, a flashy gangster-influencer type. Both have limited screen time — roughly 15 minutes — but their presence brings an instant jolt of star power.

"Khan appears to enjoy himself roasting kebabs in a pinstripe suit — somehow, he looks more relaxed than in his last solo outing, Sikandar."

— Hollywood Reporter India

The Mumbai chapter features an autorickshaw chase filmed in a frenetic GoPro style and culminates in what the Hollywood Reporter called "bizarrely hectic" fashion. The city itself was recreated on Riyadh sound stages, a detail that critics noted produced an unconvincing facsimile.

Spectacle Over Substance

Critics have been largely consistent in their verdict: 7 Dogs delivers on scale but falls short on story. Filmfare described it as "pure mayhem at full blast" and praised the ensemble while noting the plot "doesn't always make complete sense." Variety India was blunter, calling it "all bark and no bite."

The Hollywood Reporter India's review was the most cutting: "This approach struck me not as a signature style but a lazy default; it betrays a lack of faith in the plot, or in the pulse and inventiveness of the action choreography."

Giancarlo Esposito's role as the main antagonist Roman Marks drew particular criticism for being underwritten. Variety India noted the script "gives him shockingly little substance to work with, squandering his menacing potential long before the credits roll."

Camerawork Draws Praise

Where 7 Dogs earns genuine respect is in its technical craft. Cinematographer Robrecht Heyvaert and editor Pieter Smet deliver relentlessly inventive visuals — an opening Shanghai battle filmed from under a glass floor, split-screen transitions, and a large-scale desert climax packed with ATVs and luxury supercars.

Monica Bellucci's performance as Giulia Leone, the American Dog, has also been singled out for praise. A poker sequence between her character and Ezz's Khalid was compared to the Casino Royale dynamic, though it predictably devolves into gunfire.

A Sequel Setup

The film ends with a twist that clearly sets up a sequel, with Khalid preparing to retire into married life before a final rug-pull. Whether audiences will return for round two depends on their appetite for spectacle-first filmmaking.

"7 Dogs has the deep pockets, the sprawling gloss and the marquee names. What it completely lacks is a coherent script, emotional weight and performances that match the repute of its stellar ensemble."

— Variety India

The film is currently playing in Indian theatres in Hindi and English. It marks a significant statement about Saudi Arabia's ambitions to position Riyadh as a global film production hub, even if the debut effort prioritises flash over finesse.
